notes.1: (a) Only the strongest candidates were able to give a clear and precise definition of the term. Some provided vague statements stating that economies of scale were advantages of being a large business or offered examples. Such answers could not be awarded as they did not explain the term. (b) Many candidates understood that quality control involved checking the work done. Better candidates were able to provide a clear and precise definition. There were two common errors. Some confused the term with quality assurance. Others outlined why quality control was used rather than define the term. (c) Most candidate could identify one reason. Typical answers included level of output and flexibility. Only the best responses gained both the application marks available by using different points from the case to illustrate points made. Weaker responses simply restated words from the case material without identifying a reason. A number of candidates incorrectly identified reasons for using flow production. 0450 Business Studies June 2019 (d) This question proved challenging to some candidates. The most successful candidates made good use of the information provided and explained how knowledge of Maslow’s Hierarchy of needs could be used to help motivate employees in this tea factory. Many candidates were able to identify ways but were not able to develop the point to show the link between the way and the appropriate level of Maslow’s theory. Instead, they simply restated the question by saying it would increase motivation. Others were not able to apply their answer to the scenario. (e) This question caused some confusion. Better answers developed points made and were able to use the case material to support their answer. The strongest responses identified one or two ways and then discussed the potential advantages and disadvantages of using the approach before coming to a justified conclusion as to an appropriate way. Introducing new technology and training were the most popular options. Weaker candidates identified a range of ways without developing their answer to show why it might be suitable to use. A number of candidates misread this question and identified ways which were not appropriate.
notes.2: (a) The term wholesaler was not generally well understood. Few candidates were able to provide a clear and precise definition. A common error was to assume that they sold in bulk rather than breaking into bulk. Others confused the term with a manufacturer who sold direct to retailers or customers. (b) Well answered by most candidates. (c) The impact of an import quota was the better understood term in this question. Most knew this involved a limit on the number of goods which could be brought into the country. Of those that attempted to apply their answers, some repeated the same application for both points which can only be awarded once. Weaker candidates struggled to provide a clear effect of a tariff on exports as points such as ‘lose money’ or ‘costly’ were too vague to be credited. A number of candidates did not attempt this question. (d) The majority of candidates could identify either an advantage or disadvantage, but many were not able to fully develop their answers. Better candidates did attempt to apply their answer to the scenario. The best responses were able to show how points such as entering new markets or the cost of additional market research could be helpful or not to this toy making business. Instead of development, weaker answers simply repeated the knowledge point or restated the same application for both points. (e) This question proved challenging for a number of candidates. Good knowledge was evident in many responses. Better answers used the information well to support points made. These responses recognised that as the business operated in a competitive market the lack of marketing promotion was likely to result in fewer sales especially if competitors continued to advertise during this time. Weaker candidates identified a number of points but did not develop them. Some candidates did attempt to make a decision but were not always able to offer supporting reasons to back up the statement made. Some misread the question to focus on alternative ways to meet the increase in demand or discussed the merits of developing new products. Such responses could not be credited as they did not answer the question set.
notes.3: (a) Most candidates could identify one feature of a sole trader business. A common error was to identify features which could apply to any private sector business. (b) Well answered by most candidates. (c) This question produced a range of responses. Some candidates understood that that the ability to repay was likely to be an important factor for a supplier to consider when deciding whether to offer trade credit. Only the strongest responses attempted to link their answer to the scenario. Many repeated the same factor for both points. 0450 Business Studies June 2019 (d) This question differentiated well between candidates. The most successful candidates were able to identify relevant ways that a new gift shop might use a business plan. Only the best answers were able to develop points as outlined in the mark scheme to show how having a business plan might be beneficial. Weaker candidates struggled to apply their answer. Instead of development others simply repeated the knowledge point already identified. (e) Cashflow is a topic of the syllabus that continues to be misunderstood by candidates. Although many candidates were aware of relevant factors only the most able candidates were able to develop points, such as inaccurate data or cash inflows are increasing, to show why such issues were important when deciding whether to start up the new business. Evaluation was generally weak or not attempted. The weaker answers simply described Table 1 and noted points of increase and decrease. Such answers gained two marks. Others incorrectly assumed that the cashflow forecast estimated changes in profit. A number of candidates did not attempt this question.
notes.4: (a) Very few candidates were able to provide a clear and precise definition of this term. Some answers recognised one element such as it was formed by people with a common interest. A common error was to identify the actions a pressure group might take. Others confused the term with trade union or incorrectly assumed a pressure group had the power to introduce new legal controls. A number of candidates did not attempt this question. (b) Most candidates could identify one advantage of selling to a mass market. A common error was to repeat the same instead of identifying two separate advantages. (c) Many candidates were comfortable with the concept of stakeholder. The strongest answers identified two relevant stakeholder groups and were able to link their answer to the context. Weaker answers repeated the same application point or provided general answers which could apply to any business. A number of candidates did not attempt this question. (d) The concept of communication was clearly understood. Better candidates were able to effectively show why methods such as phone call and email might be appropriate for a business to use with suppliers based in other countries. Weaker candidates did not attempt to apply their answer to the scenario. There were three common errors. Some candidates did not identify a specific method and discussed verbal or written methods in general. Others included disadvantages which the question did not require. Instead of development, a small number of candidates used vague statements such as ‘cheaper’ and ‘quicker’. Such points could not be awarded. (e) Many candidates showed good knowledge of issues and were able to apply their answers to the scenario. Better answers tried to develop points to show the possible impact of issues such as lower inventory costs and different quality standards. For example different standards might increase costs as quality needed to be checked. Weaker answers identified points but did not develop them. The strongest candidates concluded that the negative impact on reputation was probably not worth the risk as the loss of sales from being associated with unethical suppliers could outweigh the benefits gained from lower costs. Often evaluation marks were not awarded as candidates often simply made an unsupported decision or restated points previously made in their answers. 0450 Business Studies June 2019 BUSINESS STUDIES
